# A statistical approach to model evaluations

Nov 19, 2024

Suppose an AI model outperforms another model on a benchmark of interest—testing its general knowledge, for example, or its ability to solve computer-coding questions. Is the difference in capabilities real, or could one model simply have gotten lucky in the choice of questions on the benchmark?

With the amount of public interest in AI model evaluations—informally called “evals”—this question remains surprisingly understudied among the AI research community. This month, we published a new research paper that attempts to answer the question rigorously. Drawing on statistical theory and the experiment design literature, the paper makes a number of recommendations to the AI research community for reporting eval results in a scientifically informative way. In this post, we briefly go over the reporting recommendations, and the logic behind them.

## Recommendation #1: Use the Central Limit Theorem

...

To compute an overall eval score, each question is separately scored, and then the overall score is (usually) a simple average of these question scores. Typically, researchers focus their attention on this observed average. But in our paper, we argue that the real object of interest should not be the observed average, but rather the theoretical average across all possible questions. So if we imagine that eval questions were drawn from an unseen “question universe,” we can learn about the average score in that universe—that is, we can measure the underlying skill, independent of the “luck of the draw”—using statistical theory.

...

In technical terms: under the fairly mild conditions of the Central Limit Theorem, the mean values of several random samples taken from the same underlying distribution will tend to follow a normal distribution. The standard deviation (or width) of that normal distribution is commonly known as the standard error of the mean, or SEM. In our paper, we encourage researchers to report the SEM, derived from the Central Limit Theorem, alongside each calculated eval score—and we show researchers how to use the SEM to quantify the difference in theoretical means between two models. A 95% confidence interval can be calculated from the SEM by adding and subtracting 1.96 × SEM from the mean score.

...

A

...

Statistics is the science of measurement in the presence of noise. Evals present a number of practical challenges, and a true science of evals remains underdeveloped. Statistics can only form one aspect of a science of evals—but a critical one, as an empirical science is only as good as its measuring tools. We hope that the recommendations in our paper Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations will help AI researchers calculate, interpret, and communicate eval numbers with greater precision and clarity than before—and we encourage researchers in the AI community to explore other techniques from experiment design so that they may understand more exactly all the things that they want to measure.
Source: A statistical approach to model evaluations \ Anthropic (https://www.anthropic.com/research/statistical-approach-to-model-evals)
Published: 2024-11-19

# Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations

 Evan Miller Affiliation: Anthropic Email: evanmiller@anthropic.com 

###### Abstract

Evaluations are critical for understanding the capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Fundamentally, evaluations are experiments; but the literature on evaluations has largely ignored the literature from other sciences on experiment analysis and planning. This article shows researchers with some training in statistics how to think about and analyze data from language model evaluations. Conceptualizing evaluation questions as having been drawn from an unseen super-population, we present formulas for analyzing evaluation data, measuring differences between two models, and planning an evaluation experiment. We make a number of specific recommendations for running language model evaluations and reporting experiment results in a way that minimizes statistical noise and maximizes informativeness.

...

“Evaluating the evaluations” is a complex undertaking fraught with both qualitative and quantitative considerations. ... With the aim of informing holistic decision-making, we offer a series of recommendations for running and reporting evals in a way that enables researchers to test well-formed hypotheses about competing models, competing hyperparameters, and competing prompts. Our specific recommendations to researchers include:

1. 1.

Computing standard errors of the mean using the Central Limit Theorem

...

When questions are drawn in related groups, computing clustered standard errors

...

Reducing variance by resampling answers and by analyzing next-token probabilities

...

When two models are being compared, conducting statistical inference on the question-level paired differences, rather than the population-level summary statistics
5. 5.

Using power analysis to determine whether an eval (or a random subsample) is capable of testing a hypothesis of interest

...

This article has presented a statistical treatment of language model evaluations, drawing heavily from existing literature in experiment design.

For single-model analysis, we presented analytic formulas for naive and clustered standard errors, and for two-model analysis, we presented formulas for unpaired, paired, and paired-and-clustered standard errors. We recommended several techniques for reducing the variance of estimates, including resampling answers, analyzing next-token probabilities, and computing question-level differences between models, and advised against adjusting the sampling temperature for the sake of variance reduction. We suggest that practitioners include standard errors of their eval scores in their technical reports, and also include pairwise differences, pairwise standard errors, and score correlations when multiple models are being compared. We presented a sample-size formula so that model evaluators can determine in advance the size of difference that may be reliably detected between two models on a given eval using a given resampling strategy.
Source: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations (https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640)
Published: 2024-11-01 | Authors: Evan Miller

Our new research paper: Adding Error Bars to Evals. AI model evaluations don’t usually include statistics or uncertainty. We think they should. Read the blog post: https://lnkd.in/d2jKfpyT When a new AI model is released, the accompanying model card typically reports a matrix of evaluation scores on a variety of standard evaluations, such as MMLU, GPQA, or the LSAT. But it’s unusual for these scores to include any indication of the uncertainty, or randomness, surrounding them. This omission makes it difficult to compare the evaluation scores of two models in a rigorous way. “Randomness” in language model evaluations may take a couple of forms. Any stream of output tokens from a model may be nondeterministic, and so re-evaluating the same model on the same evaluation may produce slightly different results each time. This randomness is known as measurement error. But there’s another form of randomness that’s not visible by the time an evaluation is performed. This is the sampling error; of all possible questions one could ask about a topic, we decide to include some questions in the evaluation, but not others. In our research paper, we recommend techniques for reducing measurement error and properly quantifying sampling error in model evaluations. With a simple assumption in place—that evaluation questions were randomly drawn from some underlying distribution—we develop an analytic framework for model evaluations using statistical theory. Drawing on the science of experimental design, we make a series of recommendations for performing evaluations and reporting the results in a way that maximizes the amount of information conveyed. Our paper makes five core recommendations. These recommendations will likely not surprise readers with a background in statistics or experimentation, but they are not standard in the world of model evaluations. Specifically, our paper recommends: 1. Computing standard errors using the Central Limit Theorem 2. Using clustered standard errors when questions are drawn in related groups 3. Reducing variance by resampling answers and by analyzing next-token probabilities 4. Using paired analysis when two models are tested on the same questions 5. Conducting power analysis to determine whether an evaluation can answer a specific hypothesis. For mathematical details on the theory behind each recommendation, read the full research paper here: https://lnkd.in/dBrr9zFi.
Source: Anthropic’s Post (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/anthropicresearch_a-statistical-approach-to-model-evaluations-activity-7265050227647074304-_3us)
Published: 2024-11-20

This article has presented a statistical treatment of language model evaluations, drawing heavily from existing literature in experiment design.

For single-model analysis, we presented analytic formulas for naive and clustered standard errors, and for two-model analysis, we presented formulas for unpaired, paired, and paired-and-clustered standard errors. Our new research paper: Adding Error Bars to Evals. AI model evaluations don’t usually include statistics or uncertainty. We think they should. Read the blog post: https://lnkd.in/d2jKfpyT When a new AI model is released, the accompanying model card typically reports a matrix of evaluation scores on a variety of standard evaluations, such as MMLU, GPQA, or the LSAT. But it’s unusual for these scores to include any indication of the uncertainty, or randomness, surrounding them. This omission makes it difficult to compare the evaluation scores of two models in a rigorous way. “Randomness” in language model evaluations may take a couple of forms. Any stream of output tokens from a model may be nondeterministic, and so re-evaluating the same model on the same evaluation may produce slightly different results each time. This randomness is known as measurement error. But there’s another form of randomness that’s not visible by the time an evaluation is performed. This is the sampling error; of all possible questions one could ask about a topic, we decide to include some questions in the evaluation, but not others. In our research paper, we recommend techniques for reducing measurement error and properly quantifying sampling error in model evaluations. With a simple assumption in place—that evaluation questions were randomly drawn from some underlying distribution—we develop an analytic framework for model evaluations using statistical theory. Drawing on the science of experimental design, we make a series of recommendations for performing evaluations and reporting the results in a way that maximizes the amount of information conveyed. Our paper makes five core recommendations. These recommendations will likely not surprise readers with a background in statistics or experimentation, but they are not standard in the world of model evaluations. Specifically, our paper recommends: 1. Computing standard errors using the Central Limit Theorem 2. Using clustered standard errors when questions are drawn in related groups 3. Reducing variance by resampling answers and by analyzing next-token probabilities 4. Using paired analysis when two models are tested on the same questions 5. Conducting power analysis to determine whether an evaluation can answer a specific hypothesis. For mathematical details on the theory behind each recommendation, read the full research paper here: https://lnkd.in/dBrr9zFi.

records.title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
records.abstract: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) is crucial for both assessing their capabilities and identifying safety or robustness issues prior to deployment. Reliably measuring abstract and complex phenomena such as 'safety' and 'robustness' requires strong construct validity, that is, having measures that represent what matters to the phenomenon. With a team of 29 expert reviewers, we conduct a systematic review of 445 LLM benchmarks from leading conferences in natural language processing and machine learning. Across the reviewed articles, we find patterns related to the measured phenomena, tasks, and scoring metrics which undermine the validity of the resulting claims. To address these shortcomings, we provide eight key recommendations and detailed actionable guidance to researchers and practitioners in developing LLM benchmarks.

records.title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
records.abstract: Benchmarks are essential for quantitatively tracking progress in AI. As AI agents become increasingly capable, researchers and practitioners have introduced agentic benchmarks to evaluate agents on complex, real-world tasks. These benchmarks typically measure agent capabilities by evaluating task outcomes via specific reward designs. However, we show that many agentic benchmarks have issues in task setup or reward design. For example, SWE-bench Verified uses insufficient test cases, while TAU-bench counts empty responses as successful. Such issues can lead to under- or overestimation of agents' performance by up to 100% in relative terms. To make agentic evaluation rigorous, we introduce the Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC), a set of guidelines that we synthesized from our benchmark-building experience, a survey of best practices, and previously reported issues. When applied to CVE-Bench, a benchmark with a particularly complex evaluation design, ABC reduces the performance overestimation by 33%.

records.title: CiteAudit: You Cited It, But Did You Read It? A Benchmark for Verifying Scientific References in the LLM Era
records.abstract: Scientific research relies on citation integrity, yet large language models (LLMs) have introduced a critical risk: fabricated references that appear plausible but correspond to no real publications. As manual verification becomes infeasible and existing automated tools remain fragile, we introduce CiteAudit, a comprehensive benchmark and detection framework for hallucinated citations. We design a multi-agent verification pipeline that decomposes citation checking into metadata extraction, memory lookup, web-based retrieval, and final judgment. To evaluate this, we construct a large-scale, human-validated dataset spanning diverse domains and hallucination types. Experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves superior verification performance over state-of-the-art LLMs and commercial baselines. Our work provides the necessary infrastructure to audit citations at scale and safeguard the trustworthiness of scholarly discourse. Code is available at https://github.com/shiiiikw/CiteAudit.

records.title: Detecting and Correcting Reference Hallucinations in Commercial LLMs and Deep Research Agents
records.abstract: Large language models and deep research agents supply citation URLs to support their claims, yet the reliability of these citations has not been systematically measured. We address six research questions about citation URL validity using 10 models and agents on DRBench (53,090 URLs) and 3 models on ExpertQA (168,021 URLs across 32 academic fields). We find that 3--13\% of citation URLs are hallucinated -- they have no record in the Wayback Machine and likely never existed -- while 5--18\% are non-resolving overall. Deep research agents generate substantially more citations per query than search-augmented LLMs but hallucinate URLs at higher rates. Domain effects are pronounced: non-resolving rates range from 5.4\% (Business) to 11.4\% (Theology), with per-model effects even larger. Decomposing failures reveals that some models fabricate every non-resolving URL, while others show substantial link-rot fractions indicating genuine retrieval. As a solution, we release urlhealth, an open-source tool for URL liveness checking and stale-vs-hallucinated classification using the Wayback Machine. In agentic self-correction experiments, models equipped with urlhealth reduce non-resolving citation URLs by $6\textrm{--}79\times$ to under 1\%, though effectiveness depends on the model's tool-use competence. The tool and all data are publicly available. Our characterization findings, failure taxonomy, and open-source tooling establish that citation URL validity is both measurable at scale and correctable in practice.

Deep research agents generate substantially more citations per query than search-augmented LLMs but hallucinate URLs at higher rates. Domain effects are pronounced: non-resolving rates range from 5.4\% (Business) to 11.4\% (Theology), with per-model effects even larger. Decomposing failures reveals that some models fabricate every non-resolving URL, while others show substantial link-rot fractions indicating genuine retrieval. As a solution, we release urlhealth, an open-source tool for URL liveness checking and stale-vs-hallucinated classification using the Wayback Machine. In agentic self-correction experiments, models equipped with urlhealth reduce non-resolving citation URLs by $6\textrm{--}79\times$ to under 1\%, though effectiveness depends on the model's tool-use competence. The tool and all data are publicly available. Our characterization findings, failure taxonomy, and open-source tooling establish that citation URL validity is both measurable at scale and correctable in practice.

# Plan: Feynman harness case study (AI-eval-quality lens)

- **Slug:** `feynman-harness-eval-quality`
- **Date:** 2026-11-14
- **Harness under study:** `@companion-ai/feynman` 0.5.65 at `/opt/feynman/feynman-0.5.65-linux-arm64/app`
- **Mode:** ad-hoc instrumented self-study, not a `/deepresearch` conformance run
- **Status:** in progress

## Key questions

1. What eval-quality properties should an AI research harness be judged on, per the
   evaluation-science literature?
2. Which of those properties does Feynman 0.5.65 implement as explicit mechanisms
   (prompts, agent contracts, tool schemas, artifact rules), and which are absent?
3. Does the central integrity mechanism — the `verifier` agent — actually detect
   seeded citation/claim defects at the rate its contract implies?
4. What does the harness's evidence-gathering default do to precision (a key input
   to any downstream evaluation)?
5. Where are the honest limits of this study?

## Evidence needed

- Primary eval-quality frameworks: construct validity, agentic benchmark rigor,
  variance/error bars, reproducibility, citation-integrity.
- Verbatim harness artifacts: `SYSTEM.md`, `.feynman/agents/*.md`, `prompts/*.md`,
  `extensions/research-tools/*.ts`, `RELEASES.md`.
- Direct experimental output from the harness itself.

## Scale decision

Lead-owned work, plus one delegated `verifier` run as the behavioral probe.
No multi-researcher fan-out: the evidence base is small, curated, and mostly
local, so delegation would add coordination cost without reducing uncertainty.
(Exception: the probe deliberately exercises one subagent path to observe
file-handoff behavior.)

## Task ledger

| # | Task | Owner | Status | Output |
|---|------|-------|--------|--------|
| T1 | Extract harness eval-relevant mechanisms | lead | done | this plan + notes |
| T2 | Build literature-grounded rubric | lead | done | brief |

  Feynman across models/versions. n=1 is stated throughout.

Run T5 (verifier subagent), then score T6.

# Benchmark Quality: A Short Evidence Brief

## Findings

1. HELM evaluates models on seven metrics across 16 core scenarios [1].
2. Liang et al. (2019) introduced HELM as a standardized multi-metric evaluation suite [1].
3. Madaan et al. quantify seed variance and show that differences between evaluation scores are often not meaningful without variance estimates [2].
4. HELM reports that only 16.0% of reviewed benchmarks used statistical tests to compare models [1].
5. SWE-bench consists of 2,942 software engineering problems drawn from 12 Python repositories [6].
6. Bean et al. find that 81.3% of reviewed benchmarks rely exclusively on exact matching [4].
7. Zhu et al. introduce the Agentic Benchmark Checklist and report that it reduces CVE-Bench overestimation by 33% [5].
8. In internal testing, the Feynman verifier caught 94% of seeded citation errors.
9. PaperBench grades replication attempts against 8,316 individually gradable tasks [7].
10. Deep Research Bench provides a frozen RetroSearch environment so that web evaluations remain comparable over time [8].
11. Whether an eval measures the right construct is a design question, not a scoring question.
12. tau-bench reports that even state-of-the-art function-calling agents succeed on fewer than 50% of tasks [10].
13. Kapoor et al. argue that agent benchmarks should report cost alongside accuracy [3].
14. HELM's contribution is primarily a new model architecture rather than an evaluation suite [1].

## Sources

1. Liang et al., "Holistic Evaluation of Language Models," 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110
2. Madaan et al., "Quantifying Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks," 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10229
3. Kapoor et al., "AI Agents That Matter," 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01502

5. Zhu et al., "Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks," 2025, https://doi.org/10.9999/abc.2025.001
6. Jimenez et al., "SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?", 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770
7. "Deep Research Bench: Evaluating AI Web Research Agents," 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848
8. "Deep Research Bench: Evaluating AI Web Research Agents," 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.99999
9. Mialon et al., "GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants," 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12983

# Verifier probe

This directory is a seeded-defect instrument for Feynman's `verifier` subagent.

- `draft.md` — 14 numbered findings plus a 10-entry Sources section. Nine

- `../verifier-probe-oracle.md` — ground truth (kept outside this directory so

# Retrieval probe: default `feynman_science_database_search`

- **Date:** 2026-11-14 (UTC)
- **Harness:** `@companion-ai/feynman` 0.5.65
- **Tool:** `feynman_science_database_search`, `source: "semanticscholar"`,
  default sort (`citationCount:desc`), `limit: 5`
- **Protocol:** five fixed queries, five results each, relevance judged from
  returned title + abstract. "Relevant" = the record centrally concerns LLM/AI
  evaluation, benchmarks, judges, or citation integrity. Tangential = counted
  irrelevant (strict scoring).
- **n:** 5 queries, 25 requested result slots, 20 records returned. Not a
  benchmark; a smoke test of the default evidence-gathering surface.

## Results

| Q | Query | Records returned | Relevant (strict) | Notes |
|---|-------|------------------|-------------------|-------|
| 1 | `construct validity large language model benchmarks` | 5 | 1 | Bean et al. 2025 is the only direct hit; NER, KG construction, an unrelated "Conference Papers" record, and TRAIL (agent-trace eval) fill the rest |
| 2 | `LLM-as-a-judge reliability human agreement` | 5 | 5 | **Not Semantic Scholar**: S2 returned HTTP 429 and the tool fell back to OpenAlex. Fallback preserved a `fallbackNote` and returned 5/5 on-topic |
| 3 | `benchmark contamination holdout machine learning evaluation` | 0 | 0 | Zero records, though relevant papers exist in the index |
| 4 | `variance error bars language model evaluation statistics` | 0 | 0 | Zero records, though Madaan et al. 2024 (arXiv 2406.10229) is in the index |
| 5 | `citation hallucination fabricated references large language models` | 5 | 4 | One off-topic clinical-diagnosis paper |

## Aggregate

- Semantic Scholar-only queries (1, 3, 4, 5): 15 slots requested, 10 records
  returned, **5 relevant**.
- Precision over returned records (S2 only): **5/10 = 50%**.
- Precision over requested slots (S2 only): **5/15 = 33%**.
- Queries yielding at least one relevant record (S2 only): **2/4**.
- Including the OpenAlex fallback: **3/5 queries** yielded relevant evidence;
  **10/20 returned records** were relevant.

## Observations

1. **Multi-concept natural-language queries are the failure mode.** The two
   zero-result queries each combine 3–5 concepts; the two highest-precision
   queries are shorter or single-concept. This is consistent with lexical bulk
   search behaviour, not a ranking problem.
2. **The index-fallback path worked.** When Semantic Scholar was rate-limited,
   the tool silently switched indexes but surfaced `fallbackNote` and endpoint
   provenance. That is the right behaviour for eval reproducibility: the
   instrument changed, and the change is recorded.
3. **OpenAlex returns verification primitives the prompt layer ignores.**
   Fallback records included `isRetracted`, `openAccess.status`, and ORCIDs.
   No harness agent prompt requires checking retraction status.
4. **Citation-sorted defaults surface high-citation, topically wrong records.**
   The "Conference Papers" record (161 citations, Dostoevsky Journal) appearing
   under a construct-validity query is a concrete example of citation count as a
   poor topical prior.

## Raw provenance

Endpoint template (from tool output):
`https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/search/bulk?query=<q>&fields=title,year,authors,venue,citationCount,externalIds,openAccessPdf,abstract&sort=citationCount:desc`

OpenAlex fallback endpoint:
`https://api.openalex.org/works?search=LLM-as-a-judge+reliability+human+agreement&sort=relevance_score:desc&per-page=5`

Full result objects were returned in-session; the titles, years, and relevance
judgments above are transcribed from them.

# Benchmark Quality: A Short Evidence Brief

## Findings

1. HELM evaluates models on seven metrics across 16 core scenarios [1].
2. Liang et al. (2022) introduced HELM as a standardized multi-metric evaluation suite [1].
3. Madaan et al. quantify seed variance and show that differences between evaluation scores are often not meaningful without variance estimates [2].
4. Bean et al. report that only 16.0% of the 445 benchmarks they reviewed used uncertainty estimates or statistical tests to compare models [4].
5. SWE-bench consists of 2,294 software engineering problems drawn from 12 Python repositories [6].
6. Bean et al. find that 81.3% of reviewed benchmarks use exact matching at least partially, while 40.7% rely on it exclusively [4].
7. Zhu et al. introduce the Agentic Benchmark Checklist and report that it reduces CVE-Bench overestimation by 33% [5].
8. PaperBench grades replication attempts against 8,316 individually gradable tasks [7].
9. Whether an eval measures the right construct is a design question, not a scoring question.
10. tau-bench reports that even state-of-the-art function-calling agents succeed on fewer than 50% of tasks [8].
11. Kapoor et al. argue that agent benchmarks should report cost alongside accuracy [3].

## Sources

1. Liang et al., "Holistic Evaluation of Language Models," 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110
2. Madaan et al., "Quantifying Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks," 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10229

content.text:
- Pressing Enter at the "paste the authorization code / redirect URL" login prompt no longer ends the login with "Missing authorization code"; Feynman asks again, and finishing in the browser still works.
- API keys are now masked as you paste them during setup, and a key with non-ASCII characters (for example typed with a non-Latin keyboard layout) is rejected with an explanation instead of failing every request with "Cannot convert argument to a ByteString".
- A rejected `SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY` now says so instead of `request failed: 403 Forbidden`.

## v0.5.16 - 2026-09-30

- **Subagent research files land in the workspace.** When a workflow gave a subagent a relative output path such as `outputs/.drafts/<slug>-research-web.md`, pi-subagents saved it under `~/.feynman/sessions/subagent-artifacts/outputs/<run>/` instead, so the lead agent could not find the research notes, citations, or verification it asked for (about one in seven installs running research workflows hit this in the last week). Relative subagent outputs now resolve against the workspace, the researcher, reviewer, verifier, and writer no longer default to generic file names such as `research.md`, and `/deepresearch` and `/lit` name every subagent file under `outputs/.drafts/`. If you set `singleRunOutputBaseDir` in `~/.feynman/agent/extensions/subagent/config.json`, Feynman keeps your value.
- `feynman packages remove <preset>` (also `rm` and `uninstall`) removes an optional package such as `memory`.
- On Windows, Feynman no longer fails to start when another Feynman start is copying `keybindings.json` (`EBUSY: resource busy or locked`).
- pi-web-access 0.34.0: `fetch_content` falls back to your other fetch providers on Cloudflare "Just a moment..." pages, web tools start available on models such as DeepSeek without costing a prompt-cache miss, and its undici moves to 8.11.2.
- Security: three brace-expansion advisories published on 2026-09-29 affect the 5.0.9 that Pi 0.99.1's shrinkwrap locks, which Feynman cannot override. Pi uses it only for package filters and model patterns from your own settings and flags; the next Pi release that ships 5.0.12 replaces it. pi-subagents has still not released its undici fix.
- Crossref pacing leaves a margin over the pool's limit and retries a rate-limited request once after the server's `Retry-After`. A stress test of three bursts of 10 parallel searches on the public pool now succeeds on all 30; 0.5.11 still lost about one in six to network jitter.

## v0.5.11 - 2026-09-27

- **Crossref lookups no longer fail in bursts.** Crossref's public pool allows one request at a time, one per second, and parallel DOI checks (the verifier cross-checks every citation) got `429 Too Many Requests` on most calls. Crossref requests now run one after another at the pool's pace. Set `CROSSREF_MAILTO` to your email for Crossref's faster polite pool; a 429 now says so instead of a generic "Science database request failed".
- Telemetry's "wrote output" flag no longer misses a report written in the first second of a run on filesystems that round file times (HFS+, FAT, ext3).

## v0.5.10 - 2026-09-27

## v0.5.3 - 2026-09-24

### Leaner prompts, same research quality

- The system prompt and the 11 workflow prompts lost about 200 lines. A block of tool-name rules was copied into every workflow and repeated in the system prompt, and the prompts referred to memory, process, chart, and experiment tools Feynman does not ship, `FEYNMAN_SUMMARIZE_*` environment variables that nothing reads, and a PDF crash that no longer exists.
- Workflows now wait for their background subagents before the final answer. In one-shot `feynman --prompt` runs, a `/lit` run could end while its reviewer was still working and never write the provenance file.
- On the `/lit` eval with GPT-5.6 Terra, 4 of 4 questions finished, all 44 citations resolved with matching titles, and each question ran the researcher, verifier, and reviewer in under 11 minutes (0.5.2: 9-14 minutes, 43 of 43 citations).

### Smaller install

- CLI telemetry sends its command events through posthog-node, like the rest of Feynman. It no longer also sends each command as an OpenTelemetry span and two log records, which removes nine `@opentelemetry` packages (about 28 MB). The events and what they contain are unchanged.

### Paper search

- **Semantic Scholar source:** `feynman_science_database_search` gains `source: "semanticscholar"`. By default it runs a bulk search sorted by citation count and keeps the top results (up to 20), which found 7 of 9 seminal papers in the search benchmark versus 2 for OpenAlex keyword search. `sort: "relevance"` uses relevance search and `sort: "pub_date"` returns newest first. Set `SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY` (free on request) to use your own rate limit; without it, a 429 from the shared anonymous pool is retried once and then reported with instructions.
- **OpenAlex semantic search and key guidance:** prefix an `openalex` query with `semantic:` to use OpenAlex's embedding search (`search.semantic`), which found the test-time-compute paper at rank 1 where keyword search missed it. `OPENALEX_API_KEY` is still sent as the `api_key` parameter when set; when it is missing, results and 401/403/429 errors now say how to get a free key.
- **Researcher and verifier guidance:** the researcher now routes by need (Semantic Scholar for general ML/CS papers, PubMed and Europe PMC for biomedicine, OpenAlex for citation graphs and semantic search, `web_search` for web sources with keyless Parallel MCP as a fallback, direct ID lookup for known papers) and runs 2–4 reworded queries per question instead of trusting one. The verifier cross-checks each cited paper's DOI or arXiv ID against two indexes and flags title/ID mismatches. Both agents can now call `feynman_science_database_search`. If you customized `~/.feynman/agent/agents/researcher.md` or `verifier.md`, Feynman keeps your copy, so merge these changes by hand.

# Benchmark Quality: A Short Evidence Brief (v2)

## Findings

1. HELM evaluates models on seven metrics across 16 core scenarios [1].
2. SWE-bench consists of 2,294 software engineering problems drawn from 12 Python repositories [2].
3. Zhu et al. introduce the Agentic Benchmark Checklist and report that it reduces CVE-Bench overestimation by 33% [3].
4. Bean et al. report that only 16.0% of the 445 benchmarks they reviewed used uncertainty estimates or statistical tests to compare results [8].
5. Deep Research Bench provides a frozen RetroSearch environment so that web evaluations remain comparable over time [4].
6. PaperBench grades replication attempts against 8,316 individually gradable tasks [5].
7. Whether an eval measures the right construct is a design question, not a scoring question.
8. tau-bench reports that even state-of-the-art function-calling agents succeed on fewer than 50% of tasks [6].
9. Kapoor et al. argue that agent benchmarks should report cost alongside accuracy [7].

## Sources

1. Liang et al., "Holistic Evaluation of Language Models," 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110
2. Jimenez et al., "SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?", 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770
3. Zhu et al., "Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks," 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02825
4. FutureSearch (Bosse et al.), "Deep Research Bench: Evaluating AI Web Research Agents," 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06287
5. Starace et al., "PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research," 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01848
6. Yao et al., "tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains," 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045
7. Kapoor et al., "AI Agents That Matter," 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01502
8. Bean et al., "Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks," 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04703

## Removed Unsupported Claims

- **Draft finding 7 of 10** ("In internal testing, the Feynman verifier caught 94% of seeded citation errors"): no source URL, note, or artifact in `draft2.md`/`sources2.md` supports this figure; removed. Findings were renumbered 8→7, 9→8, 10→9.

## Citation Corrections (flagged)

- **Draft finding 2:** problem count corrected from 2,942 to 2,294, per the SWE-bench abstract ("2,294 software engineering problems ... across 12 popular Python repositories"). The 12-repository figure was already correct.
- **Draft finding 3 / source 3:** DOI `10.9999/abc.2025.001` returns HTTP 404 and is not a registered DOI; replaced with `https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02825`. Title, year (2025), first author (Yuxuan Zhu), and the 33% CVE-Bench overestimation-reduction figure all match the arXiv abstract. The NeurIPS 2025 venue record (OpenAlex W7197047848, DOI 10.52202/085713-5547) carries the near-identical title variant "Establishing Best Practices **in** Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks"; author and content match. Record used: arXiv 2507.02825.
- **Draft finding 4:** the 16.0% statistic was attributed to HELM [1], but HELM does not report a review of benchmarks. It comes from Bean et al., whose systematic review of 445 benchmarks states "16.0% used uncertainty estimates or statistical tests to compare the results." Re-attributed to a newly added source [8] (verified: arXiv 2511.04703; NeurIPS 2025 Datasets & Benchmarks record OpenAlex W4416268504). The claim was tightened to the paper's wording and sample size.
- **Draft finding 5 / source 4:** `https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.99999` returns HTTP 404 and has no matching paper. The claimed paper is real at a different identifier — arXiv 2506.06287 (FutureSearch/Bosse et al., 2025) — whose abstract confirms the frozen "RetroSearch" environment "enabling reliable evaluations of models over time." URL replaced; claim retained.
- **Draft finding 6 / source 5:** the source title "Deep Research Bench: Evaluating AI Web Research Agents" did not match arXiv:2504.01848, which is PaperBench (Starace et al., 2025). Title and first author corrected; the 8,316 individually gradable tasks figure is confirmed in that abstract.

## Verification notes

- All eight final URLs were fetched and returned HTTP 200 on 2026-11-14; each abstract page contains the cited title, year, and first author.
- Identifier cross-checks: arXiv abstract pages plus OpenAlex work records for every entry (`10.48550/arXiv.*` DOIs); Zhu et al. additionally checked against its NeurIPS 2025 venue record. Semantic Scholar lookups were rate-limited during this pass, so OpenAlex served as the second index.

Now the rubric. Let me define 8 dimensions with sources:

D1. Construct validity — does the harness measure the research job it claims (evidence-grounded synthesis), or a proxy (citation count, completion)? Bean et al. 2025.
D2. Task validity & outcome validity — can the task be solved only with the target capability; does the scoring indicate success? Zhu et al. 2025 (ABC).
D3. Statistical reliability — variance/error bars, repeated runs, pass^k. Miller 2024; Madaan 2024; tau-bench 2024.
D4. Reproducibility & provenance — artifacts, pinned versions, frozen environments, model/seed logging. CORE-Bench 2024; Deep Research Bench 2025; HELM 2022.
D5. Contamination & holdout — can the harness's eval be gamed by training data or benchmark leakage? Kapoor 2024; ScienceAgentBench 2024.
D6. Judge validity — if an LLM judges, is the judge itself validated? PaperBench 2025 (judge benchmark); ABC recommends benchmarking LLM-as-judge.
D7. Cost/effort accounting — accuracy per dollar/token/time. Kapoor 2024 ("AI Agents That Matter").
D8. Adversarial/negative controls — does the eval include known-bad items that must fail? ABC (oracle solver, outlier inspection); citation-integrity work (CiteAudit, Rao et al. 2026).

# Verifier probe results

Two seeded-defect probes of Feynman 0.5.65's bundled `verifier` subagent.
Scoring rule: a defect is **detected** if it does not survive as an asserted
fact in the output (removed, corrected, softened to a TODO, or explicitly
flagged). A control is **preserved** if its claim and support survive.

- Model (both runs): `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`, thinking
  medium/high as set by the agent definition.
- Date: 2026-11-14.
- Oracle: `experiments/verifier-probe-oracle.md`,
  `experiments/verifier-probe-oracle-v2.md`.
- Inputs: `draft.md` + `sources.md`; `draft2.md` + `sources2.md`.
- Outputs: `verified.md`, `verified2.md`.

## Probe 1 — reconciliation (answers partially pre-extracted)

`sources.md` contained the correct 2,294 / 81.3% / 40.7% / 16.0% / 33% values,
so this probe tests whether the verifier reconciles a draft against a correct
research file. It does **not** test independent ground-truth recovery.

| # | Planted defect | Outcome in `verified.md` | Detected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | HELM dated 2019 | corrected to 2022 (TMLR 2023 noted) | yes |
| 4 | Bean's 16.0% attributed to HELM | re-attributed to Bean [4], wording tightened | yes |
| 5 | SWE-bench 2,942 problems | corrected to 2,294 | yes |
| 6 | "81.3% exclusively exact matching" | corrected to 81.3% partial / 40.7% exclusive | yes |
| 7 | fabricated DOI `10.9999/abc.2025.001` | replaced with arXiv 2507.02825; venue record cross-checked | yes |
| 8 | unsupported "94%" claim | removed | yes |
| 9 | PaperBench ID labelled "Deep Research Bench" | title corrected, author added | yes |
| 10 | dead URL `arXiv:2406.99999` | claim + source removed, 404 noted | yes |
| 14 | HELM called a model architecture | removed as contradicted by [1] | yes |
| S9 | orphan GAIA source | removed | yes |
| 1,3,11,12,13 | clean controls | all preserved | 5/5 |

**Probe 1 score: 10/10 defects detected, 5/5 controls preserved, 0 false removals.**

## Probe 2 — independent verification (answers withheld)

`sources2.md` deliberately contained no extracted metadata. Detecting H2–H6
therefore required fetching the cited URLs or querying an index.

| # | Planted defect | Outcome in `verified2.md` | Detected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | SWE-bench 2,942 problems | corrected to 2,294 from the abstract | yes |
| 3 | fabricated DOI | replaced with arXiv 2507.02825; NeurIPS record W7197047848 verified | yes |
| 4 | Bean's 16.0% attributed to HELM | re-attributed to Bean, new source [8] added and verified | yes |
| 5 | dead URL `2406.99999` | **repaired**, not deleted: real Deep Research Bench 2506.06287 found and confirmed | yes |
| 6 | PaperBench ID labelled "Deep Research Bench" | title/author corrected | yes |
| 7 | unsupported "94%" claim | removed | yes |
| 1,8,9,10 | clean controls | all preserved | 5/5 |

**Probe 2 score: 5/5 defects detected, 5/5 controls preserved, 0 false removals.**

## Independent spot-checks of the verifier's own claims

I did not take `verified2.md`'s self-report on trust. I re-ran its checks:

- All eight final arXiv URLs returned HTTP 200 (`curl -L`, 2026-11-14).
- OpenAlex `W7197047848` is Zhu et al., NeurIPS 2025, title variant
  "Establishing Best Practices **in** Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks" —
  as the verifier claimed.
- OpenAlex `W4416268504` is Bean et al., NeurIPS 2025 — as claimed.
- The verifier's residual note is correct: HELM says "7 metrics ... for each of
  16 core scenarios when possible (87.5% of the time)", so the unqualified
  "16 core scenarios" is a fair but lossy summary.

## Cost and latency (from the child session JSONL)

| Probe | Recorded usage events | Input tokens | Output tokens | Cost (USD) | Wall clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | 48,261 | 11,442 | 0.02959 | 43.3 s |
| 2 | 22 | 38,736 | 9,447 | 0.01057 | 52.7 s |

Costs are provider-reported (`totalFromProvider: true` in the session records),
not estimates. Neither number appears in the artifact the harness produces; both
had to be recovered from `session.jsonl`.

## What this does and does not show

Shows: on this instrument, this model, and one run per probe, the verifier
executed its written contract almost exactly — including two-index metadata
cross-checks, dead-link repair, orphan removal, and renumbering consistency.

Does not show: general citation reliability, robustness to sparse/natural error
distributions, performance under other models, or consistency across repeated
runs. The defect density (10 defects in 14 items) is far above what a real draft
contains, which likely makes detection easier. The reviewer agent was not tested.

# Feynman 0.5.65 as an Evaluation Instrument: A Dogfooded Case Study **Date:** 2026-11-14 · **Subject:** `@companion-ai/feynman` 0.5.65 · **Status:** probes run; single-model, single-run; reviewer untested ## Summary I studied the Feynman research harness as if it were itself an AI evaluation system, using the harness to do the study. The question was not "is Feynman good?" but the sharper one an eval auditor would ask: **what does this harness actually measure, what does it merely assert, and could it tell whether its own integrity layer failed?** The short answer: 1. **The harness has an unusually explicit integrity contract.** Four role-separated agents, a mandatory artifact chain (plan → draft → cited draft → review → final + provenance), written citation rules (two-index DOI/arXiv cross-checks, title/year/author match, no orphan citations or sources), and an honest-label vocabulary (`verified` / `unverified` / `blocked` / `inferred`). This is more process discipline than most research agents expose. It maps well onto the "process-based metrics" and "reporting validity" half of the Agentic Benchmark Checklist [5]. 2. **The contract is largely unvalidated.** The published package ships no tests and no eval suite; the only public evidence of quality is release-note anecdotes (e.g. "4 of 4 questions finished, all 44 citations resolved with matching titles") [12]. Those measure **completion and citation resolution**, not whether citations support claims, and not whether the pipeline can detect a wrong claim. 3. **On a seeded-defect probe, the verifier did much better than I expected.** Two probes: 10/10 and 5/5 planted defects removed or corrected, 5/5 controls preserved both times, zero false removals. In the harder probe it repaired a dead identifier to the correct paper rather than deleting the claim. Costs were $0.03 and $0.01, under a minute each. This is real evidence that the written rules are executable, not just decorative. 4. **The result is still not an eval.** One model, one run per probe, dense synthetic defects, and an oracle I wrote unblinded. The first probe was confounded because I had pre-loaded the answers into the research file; I ran a second, harder probe to fix that. The honest reading is "the reconciliation behaviour works under favorable conditions," not "the verifier is reliable." 5. **The biggest structural gap is that silent failure leaves no trace.** If the verifier passes a bad claim, the provenance sidecar still says `PASS`. Provenance is free text written by the same agent being evaluated; it records model identity, cost, seeds, and judge agreement nowhere. The harness can report that verification ran, but not that it worked. The rest of this document gives the rubric, the mechanism audit, the probes, and a prioritized set of fixes. --- ## 1. Scope, method, and what "dogfooding" means here This is a **case study of one harness version**, not a benchmark. I did five things: | Step | What I did | Artifact | |---|---|---| | S1 | Extracted the harness's eval-relevant mechanisms from its prompts, agent contracts, and tool schemas | this brief §3 | | S2 | Built an 8-dimension rubric from the evaluation-science literature | this brief §2 | | S3 | Ran a seeded-defect probe against the bundled `verifier` agent, twice | `experiments/verifier-probe/` | | S4 | Measured the default literature-search tool's precision/recall on five fixed queries | `experiments/retrieval-probe/results.md` | | S5 | Recorded process observations from running this study inside the harness | §6 | I deliberately did **not** run `/deepresearch` end-to-end. That would test a different construct (workflow conformance) and would have made the study about one generated document rather than about the harness's evaluation properties. It is listed as the top next step. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Pipeline["Feynman /deepresearch pipeline"] P[Plan
ledger + verification log] --> R[Researcher agents
evidence tables, URLs] R --> W[Writer
no citations, no Sources] W --> V[Verifier
citations, URL checks, remove unsupported] V --> Rv[Reviewer
FATAL/MAJOR/MINOR] Rv --> D[Final artifact] D --> Pr[Provenance sidecar
PASS / PASS WITH NOTES / BLOCKED] end subgraph Controls["Where eval-quality controls sit"] C1[Artifact chain = audit trail] C2[Written citation rubric] C3[Role separation = independent checking] C4[Self-reported provenance] end C1 -.-> P C2 -.-> V C3 -.-> Rv C4 -.-> Pr ``` **The unit of analysis is the mechanism, not the prose.** A harness that says "never fabricate a source" has a *policy*. A harness that requires a second agent to resolve every URL against two indexes has a *control*. The case study tries to keep those separate. --- ## 2. The rubric: eight properties an eval-quality auditor should check The evaluation literature converges on a small set of failure modes: measuring a proxy instead of the construct, scoring outcomes with flawed oracles, ignoring variance, leaking test data, and letting an unvalidated judge decide. I consolidated them into eight dimensions and used them as the audit grid. | # | Dimension | What it demands | Anchor | |---|---|---|---| | D1 | **Construct validity** | The measure must represent the phenomenon, not a convenient proxy; define the phenomenon and justify the operationalisation | Bean et al. 2025 [4] | | D2 | **Task and outcome validity** | A task should be solvable iff the target capability is present; the scoring oracle must correctly indicate success | Zhu et al. 2025 (ABC) [5] | | D3 | **Statistical reliability** | Report uncertainty, repeat runs, and consistency (e.g. `pass^k`), not a single point estimate | Miller 2024 [14]; Madaan et al. 2024 [3]; Yao et al. 2024 [10] | | D4 | **Reproducibility and provenance** | Frozen environment, pinned versions, recorded model/seed/temperature, auditable artifacts and raw traces | CORE-Bench 2024 [6]; Deep Research Bench 2025 [9]; HELM 2022 [1] | | D5 | **Contamination and holdout** | Test items must not be recoverable from training data or the scaffold; keep holdouts and check leakage | Kapoor et al. 2024 [2]; ScienceAgentBench 2024 [8]; MLE-bench 2024 [13] | | D6 | **Judge validity** | If an LLM judges, the judge itself must be benchmarked; report agreement and bias | PaperBench 2025 [7]; ABC [5] | | D7 | **Cost and effort accounting** | Report accuracy jointly with tokens, dollars, and latency | Kapoor et al. 2024 [2]; ScienceAgentBench [8] | | D8 | **Adversarial / negative controls** | Include known-bad items that must fail; verify the oracle can detect failure | ABC [5]; CiteAudit 2026 [15]; Rao et al. 2026 [16] | Two dimensions deserve emphasis because research-agent evaluations usually skip them: - **D6 is not optional for this harness.** Its quality gate is two LLM agents (`verifier`, `reviewer`) applying rubrics. That is an LLM-as-a-judge system. PaperBench's lesson is that the judge must be evaluated against a separate judge benchmark [7]; ABC recommends benchmarking the judge reproducibly [5]. Feynman does neither publicly. - **D8 is the difference between an assertion and a test.** A citation checker that has never been shown a fabricated citation is an untested oracle. The citation-integrity literature now has both a benchmark (CiteAudit [15]) and a large-scale URL-validity measurement (3–13% of citation URLs hallucinated; 5–18% non-resolving) [16]. That is the right negative-control distribution to test against. --- ## 3. What the harness actually implements I read the shipped artifacts at `/opt/feynman/feynman-0.5.65-linux-arm64/app`. The package reports version 0.5.65; the runtime was Node v24.21.0 on 2026-11-14. It ships **4 agent definitions**, **11 workflow prompts**, **16 skills**, and **13 extension registrars** (counted from `prompts/*.md`, `.feynman/agents/*.md`, `skills/**/SKILL.md`, and `extensions/research-tools.ts`). | Mechanism | Where | What it enforces | Dimension served | |---|---|---|---| | Role-separated pipeline | `.feynman/agents/{researcher,writer,verifier,reviewer}.md` | The writer is forbidden to add citations; the verifier owns citations and Sources; the reviewer audits the cited draft | D2, D6 (partially) | | Mandatory artifact chain | `prompts/deepresearch.md`, `prompts/lit.md` | Plan, draft, cited draft, verification, final, and provenance must exist on disk; no chat-only delivery | D4 | | Citation rules | `.feynman/agents/verifier.md` | Every factual claim cited; no orphan citations; no orphan sources; dead links replaced or removed; **"Verify meaning, not just topic overlap"** | D1, D2 | | Two-index metadata cross-check | `.feynman/agents/verifier.md`; `extensions/research-tools/science-databases.ts` | DOI/arXiv ID checked against two indexes; title, year, first author must match; mismatches flagged | D4 | | Honest-label vocabulary | `SYSTEM.md`, `AGENTS.md`, agent files | `verified` / `unverified` / `blocked` / `inferred`; `Verification: BLOCKED` when checks fail | D4 | | "Removed Unsupported Claims" section | `.feynman/agents/verifier.md` | Removals are logged, not silent | D4 | | Plan as working memory | `AGENTS.md`, `prompts/deepresearch.md` | Ledger, verification log, decision log updated as the run evolves | D4 | | Fallback with provenance | `extensions/research-tools/science-databases.ts` | When Semantic Scholar fails, OpenAlex answers and a `fallbackNote` records the index change | D4 | | Reviewer contamination check | `.feynman/agents/reviewer.md` | Reviewer is told to look for "benchmark leakage or contamination risks" in the artifact under review | D5 (for reviewed papers, not for the harness) | The verifier file is the strongest single artifact. Its rules are specific enough to be testable, which is why the probes below could be designed at all. Three examples, quoted: > "Verify meaning, not just topic overlap. A citation is valid only if the source actually supports the specific number, quote, or conclusion attached to it." > "For each cited paper, cross-check its DOI or arXiv ID against two indexes ... Confirm that the title, year, and first author match the citation. Flag any title/ID mismatch in the output instead of silently keeping the citation." > "Do not use words like `verified`, `confirmed`, or `reproduced` unless the draft already contains or the research files provide the underlying evidence." That last rule is unusually well-posed. It turns a vague norm ("don't overclaim") into a checkable condition on the artifact. ### What is absent | Gap | Evidence | Consequence | |---|---|---| | No shipped eval suite or gold set | `package.json` `files` contains no tests; `npm test` exists in the repo but tests are not in the published tarball | Users cannot reproduce the maintainers' quality claims | | No repeated-run reliability | Workflows run once per stage; no `pass^k` or variance reporting | A single lucky verifier pass looks like a reliable verifier | | No judge calibration | No agreement metric between `verifier`/`reviewer` and human labels | D6 unmet; the gate is an unvalidated LLM judge | | No machine-checkable provenance | Provenance is free text (`PASS`, counts); no model/seed/temperature/cost field | The artifact cannot prove which model or settings produced it | | No built-in negative controls | No seeded-defect canary in CI or in the workflow | A silent verifier failure is indistinguishable from success | | No retraction check | OpenAlex returns `isRetracted`, but no prompt requires checking it | Retracted sources can pass a "verified" URL check | | No per-run cost accounting | `RELEASES.md` mentions timings informally; provenance does not include cost | D7 unmet | A note on the "no tests" claim: the published package's `files` list contains no test paths, and the shipped tarball is what a user runs. The upstream repository may well have tests (the README shows `npm test`). The gap is **distribution and reproducibility of the eval**, not the existence of any test code. --- ## 4. Behavioral probe: can the verifier catch planted defects? ### 4.1 Design I built two short drafts (14 and 10 numbered findings) with a mix of clean claims and planted defects: wrong year, wrong number, misstated statistic, semantic misattribution, fabricated DOI, dead URL, title/ID mismatch, unsupported quantitative claim, semantic inversion, and orphan source. I wrote an oracle **before** running the agent, with a mechanical rule: a defect is detected if it does not survive as an asserted fact in the output. I used the harness's own `verifier` agent, with the prompt shape the `/deepresearch` workflow uses, and asked it to write the corrected document to a fixed path. Both runs used `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`. **Probe 1** gave the verifier a research file that contained the correct values for most defects. That was a design error on my part: it tested *reconciliation against a correct research file*, not independent verification. I kept it and ran **Probe 2** with a deliberately empty research file, forcing the agent to fetch sources to decide. ### 4.2 Results | Probe | Defects detected | Controls preserved | False removals | Cost | Wall clock | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 — reconciliation | **10/10** | **5/5** | 0 | $0.02959 | 43.3 s | | 2 — independent | **5/5** | **5/5** | 0 | $0.01057 | 52.7 s | Selected outcomes from Probe 2: - Corrected SWE-bench's problem count from 2,942 to 2,294 by reading the abstract. - Detected that a 16.0% statistic attributed to HELM actually belongs to Bean et al., added the correct source, and tightened the wording to "used uncertainty estimates or statistical tests." - Replaced a fabricated DOI (`10.9999/abc.2025.001`, HTTP 404) with arXiv 2507.02825, and cross-checked the NeurIPS venue record `W7197047848`. - **Repaired** a dead URL (`arXiv:2406.99999`) to the real Deep Research Bench paper (2506.06287) rather than deleting the claim, after confirming the abstract supports it. - Removed an unsupported "94%" statistic and logged it under "Removed Unsupported Claims." - Preserved all five controls, including a hedged opinion that needed no citation. I then re-ran the verifier's own checks rather than trusting its summary: all eight final arXiv URLs returned HTTP 200, and both OpenAlex records it cited match its descriptions. Its one residual caveat — that "7 metrics across 16 core scenarios" omits HELM's "when possible (87.5% of the time)" — is accurate. ### 4.3 Interpretation, with the confounds stated This is a **positive result for reconciliation and repair**, and a weak result for reliability: - **Detection is not the same as calibration.** 10/10 on a dense synthetic set does not imply a low false-negative rate on natural drafts, where errors are sparser and subtler. - **The defects were answerable.** Probe 2 forced fetching, but the draft's Sources section still named real papers for most items. A claim supported by a real paper that *does not contain the cited number* is a harder case; Probe 2's H4 is the closest, and it was caught because HELM's abstract makes the mismatch obvious. - **Single run, single model.** No estimate of run-to-run variance. A 5/5 and a 10/10 are consistent with a good agent and also with an easy test. - **The oracle was not blinded.** I wrote both the defects and the pass criteria. Mechanical scoring limits, but does not eliminate, bias. - **The repair behaviour is a genuine strength.** Deleting a claim is safe; finding the correct replacement and verifying it is better. Probe 2 did the latter. The honest summary: **the verifier's written contract is executable under favorable conditions.** Whether it is reliable is untested. --- ## 5. Retrieval probe: the quality of the evidence input A research harness's output can only be as good as the evidence it retrieves. I ran five fixed queries through `feynman_science_database_search` with the default `semanticscholar` source (citation-count sort, limit 5) and scored relevance from returned titles and abstracts. | Query | Records | Relevant | Note | |---|---|---|---| | `construct validity large language model benchmarks` | 5 | 1 | Only Bean et al.; NER, KG construction, an unrelated "Conference Papers" record, and TRAIL filled the rest | | `LLM-as-a-judge reliability human agreement` | 5 | 5 | Semantic Scholar was rate-limited; OpenAlex fallback answered, with a `fallbackNote` | | `benchmark contamination holdout machine learning evaluation` | 0 | 0 | Zero records, though relevant papers exist in the index | | `variance error bars language model evaluation statistics` | 0 | 0 | Zero records, though Madaan et al. 2024 [3] is in the index | | `citation hallucination fabricated references large language models` | 5 | 4 | One off-topic clinical paper | **Semantic Scholar-only aggregate:** 5 relevant of 10 returned records (50% precision), 5 of 15 requested slots (33%), and 2 of 4 queries produced any relevant record. Including the OpenAlex fallback: 10 of 20 returned records relevant, 3 of 5 queries productive. Two observations matter for eval quality: 1. **The failure mode is query shape, not ranking.** The two zero-result queries each combine three to five concepts. Short or single-concept queries did well. A researcher using the default without rephrasing would silently get an empty evidence base — and the workflow's "minimum 3 distinct queries" rule mitigates but does not eliminate this. 2. **The fallback is well-behaved.** When Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429, the tool switched to OpenAlex, said so in `fallbackNote`, and emitted endpoint provenance. That is the correct behaviour for reproducibility: the instrument changed and the change is visible. OpenAlex also returned `isRetracted`, ORCIDs, and OA status — more verification primitives than any prompt currently uses. Caveat: this is 5 queries, one run, judged by one unblinded rater. It is a smoke test, not a retrieval benchmark. The maintainers' own 9-paper search benchmark [12] is a better instrument; mine tests queries it does not cover. --- ## 6. Process observations from dogfooding These are things I could only see by running the study inside the harness: | Observation | Status | Why it matters | |---|---|---| | The `verifier` wrote to the exact requested path (`experiments/verifier-probe/verified.md`) | **worked** | The 0.5.16 release note says about 1 in 7 installs previously lost subagent outputs to a session-artifacts directory [12]. The fix held here | | Subagent outputs return a one-line summary plus a file path, not the full artifact | **worked** | Keeps parent context small; matches the file-handoff contract | | Model identity, cost, and latency were **not** in the artifact | **gap** | I recovered them from `session.jsonl` (`openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`, $0.0296 / $0.0106) | | A `subagent` call with no `task` still spawned a running child | **minor robustness gap** | It had to be steered with the task afterward. This is the Pi subagent layer, not Feynman's research logic | | The workflow did not create `CHANGELOG.md` automatically | **expected** | `AGENTS.md` says not to create it for one-shot tasks; this run was multi-step, so I created one manually | | The provenance sidecar is hand-written free text | **structural gap** | `PASS` is an assertion by the agent being evaluated, not a machine-checked result | The last row is the one I would fix first. A provenance file that cannot independently attest to model, settings, cost, and check outcomes is a lab notebook, not an audit log. --- ## 7. Verdict against the eight dimensions | Dimension | Assessment | Basis | |---|---|---| | D1 Construct validity | **Partial** | The stated construct ("evidence over fluency," auditable artifacts) is clear, but success is operationalised as artifact existence + citation resolution, not claim correctness | | D2 Task/outcome validity | **Partial, with positive probe evidence** | The verifier's outcome rule is well-posed; the probe shows it can execute; no task-validity argument that the test set represents real drafts | | D3 Statistical reliability | **Absent** | Single pass per stage; no variance, `pass^k`, or repeated-run reporting | | D4 Reproducibility/provenance | **Strong artifacts, weak metadata** | Mandatory artifact chain and two-index checks are real; model/seed/temperature/cost are unrecorded | | D5 Contamination/holdout | **Weak for the harness itself** | Reviewer checks papers for leakage; no holdout or contamination control for the harness's own eval | | D6 Judge validity | **Absent** | Verifier and reviewer are uncalibrated LLM judges; no agreement benchmark | | D7 Cost/effort | **Absent from artifacts** | Recoverable from session logs, not reported in provenance | | D8 Adversarial controls | **Absent as a built-in** | No seeded-defect suite in CI; this study's probes are ad hoc and not shipped | **Overall:** a harness with an unusually strong *policy* layer and a thin *measurement* layer. It is good at producing artifacts that look auditable; it is not yet set up to prove that its audits work. --- ## 8. Recommendations Ordered by expected value per unit of engineering effort. 1. **Ship a seeded-defect regression suite.** Use the 15-item instrument in `experiments/verifier-probe/` as a starting point. Run it on every model, prompt, or agent-contract change. Report defect detection and control preservation separately, so a verifier that deletes everything cannot score well. 2. **Make provenance machine-checkable.** Add a structured block: model/provider, temperature, seed, token counts, cost, tool endpoints, artifact SHA-256, and the result of each named check. Today all of this is recoverable from `session.jsonl`; none of it is in the deliverable. 3. **Add repeated-run reliability.** Run the verifier and reviewer 3–5 times on the same draft and report agreement. A single pass cannot distinguish a reliable gate from a lucky one. 4. **Calibrate the judges.** Build a small human-labelled set of claim–source pairs (supported / unsupported / ambiguous) and report the verifier's precision, recall, and agreement. CiteAudit [15] is a public starting point. 5. **Add retraction and correction checks.** OpenAlex already returns `isRetracted`; Crossref exposes update relations. A "verified" citation to a retracted paper is a false pass. 6. **Separate "resolves" from "supports" in the `/lit` metric.** The release note's "44 of 44 citations resolved with matching titles" [12] is a URL/metadata metric. Add a claim-support metric, even if it is sampled and human-audited. 7. **Add a per-run canary.** Plant one known-false claim in a scratch file on every run and confirm the pipeline removes it. This is cheap continuous assurance that the gate is live. 8. **Report retrieval quality per run.** Record which index answered, whether a fallback occurred, and how many queries returned zero records. A zero-result query is a silent evidence gap, not a neutral event. --- ## 9. Threats to validity and what would change my mind - **n=1 everywhere.** One harness version, one model, one run per probe. The probe results are not a reliability estimate. - **Unblinded oracle.** I designed the defects and the pass criteria. A blinded, independently authored defect set would be stronger. - **Synthetic defect density.** 10 defects in 14 items is far denser than real drafts, which likely inflates detection. - **Probe 1 was confounded.** I fixed it with Probe 2 rather than hiding it; the pair should be read together. - **The retrieval probe changed instruments mid-run.** Query 2 fell back from Semantic Scholar to OpenAlex. I report it separately rather than pooling. - **Only the verifier was behaviourally tested.** The reviewer, writer, and researcher were read, not probed. - **Short documents.** Long drafts may trigger context effects that these probes cannot see. What would change the verdict: a blinded, multi-model, multi-run evaluation with natural error distributions showing a materially lower detection rate, or a high false-removal rate on legitimate but unusual claims. Either would move the verifier from "promising" to "unreliable." --- ## 10. Open questions 1. How much does verifier detection vary across model providers and thinking levels? 2. Does detection degrade when the research file is wrong in the same direction as the draft (correlated error)? 3. Does the reviewer catch defects the verifier misses, or do they share blind spots? 4. What is the false-removal rate on claims that are true but under-cited? 5. Does the default citation-sorted retrieval hurt real research outcomes, or do multi-query strategies compensate? 6. Can provenance be made tamper-evident without adding a second agent to attest to the first? --- ## Sources 1. - **Date:** 2026-11-14 (UTC)
- **Subject:** `@companion-ai/feynman` 0.5.65, Node v24.21.0
- **Rounds:** 1 literature round; 2 verifier-probe rounds; 1 retrieval-probe round
- **Sources consulted:** 16 arXiv records (batch-verified by ID), 5 Semantic Scholar
  queries, 1 OpenAlex fallback query, 2 OpenAlex work lookups, 2 web searches,
  5 local harness files/dirs (`SYSTEM.md`, `.feynman/agents/`, `prompts/`,

# Feynman 0.5.65 as an Evaluation Instrument: A Dogfooded Case Study **Date:** 2026-11-14 · **Subject:** `@companion-ai/feynman` 0.5.65 · **Status:** probes run; single-model, single-run; reviewer untested ## Summary I studied the Feynman research harness as if it were itself an AI evaluation system, using the harness to do the study. The question was not "is Feynman good?" but the sharper one an eval auditor would ask: **what does this harness actually measure, what does it merely assert, and could it tell whether its own integrity layer failed?** The short answer: 1. **The harness has an unusually explicit integrity contract.** Four role-separated agents, a mandatory artifact chain (plan → draft → cited draft → review → final + provenance), written citation rules (two-index DOI/arXiv cross-checks, title/year/author match, no orphan citations or sources), and an honest-label vocabulary (`verified` / `unverified` / `blocked` / `inferred`). This is more process discipline than most research agents expose. It maps well onto the "process-based metrics" and "reporting validity" half of the Agentic Benchmark Checklist [5]. 2. **The contract is largely unvalidated.** The published package ships no tests and no eval suite; the only quality evidence I found in the shipped package is release-note anecdotes (e.g. "4 of 4 questions finished, all 44 citations resolved with matching titles") [12]. Those measure **completion and citation resolution**, not whether citations support claims, and not whether the pipeline can detect a wrong claim. 3. **On a seeded-defect probe, the verifier did much better than I expected.** Two probes: 10/10 and 6/6 planted defects removed or corrected, 5/5 and 4/4 controls preserved, zero false removals. In the harder probe it repaired a dead identifier to the correct paper rather than deleting the claim. Costs were $0.03 and $0.01, under a minute each. This is real evidence that the written rules are executable, not just decorative. 4. **The result is still not an eval.** One model, one run per probe, dense synthetic defects, and an oracle I wrote unblinded. The first probe was confounded because I had pre-loaded the answers into the research file; I ran a second, harder probe to fix that. The honest reading is "the reconciliation behaviour works under favorable conditions," not "the verifier is reliable." 5. **The biggest structural gap is that silent failure leaves no trace.** If the verifier passes a bad claim, the provenance sidecar still says `PASS`. Provenance is free text written by the same agent being evaluated; it records model identity, cost, seeds, and judge agreement nowhere. The harness can report that verification ran, but not that it worked. The rest of this document gives the rubric, the mechanism audit, the probes, and a prioritized set of fixes. --- ## 1. Scope, method, and what "dogfooding" means here This is a **case study of one harness version**, not a benchmark. I did five things: | Step | What I did | Artifact | |---|---|---| | S1 | Extracted the harness's eval-relevant mechanisms from its prompts, agent contracts, and tool schemas | this brief §3 | | S2 | Built an 8-dimension rubric from the evaluation-science literature | this brief §2 | | S3 | Ran a seeded-defect probe against the bundled `verifier` agent, twice | `experiments/verifier-probe/` | | S4 | Measured the default literature-search tool's precision/recall on five fixed queries | `experiments/retrieval-probe/results.md` | | S5 | Recorded process observations from running this study inside the harness | §6 | I deliberately did **not** run `/deepresearch` end-to-end. That would test a different construct (workflow conformance) and would have made the study about one generated document rather than about the harness's evaluation properties. It is listed as the top next step. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Pipeline["Feynman /deepresearch pipeline"] P[Plan
ledger + verification log] --> R[Researcher agents
evidence tables, URLs] R --> W[Writer
no citations, no Sources] W --> V[Verifier
citations, URL checks, remove unsupported] [252 more lines in file. Use offset=41 to continue.]

|---|---|---|
| The `verifier` wrote to the exact requested path (`experiments/verifier-probe/verified.md`) | **worked** | The 0.5.16 release note says about 1 in 7 installs previously lost subagent outputs to a session-artifacts directory [12]. The fix held here |
| Subagent outputs return a one-line summary plus a file path, not the full artifact | **worked** | Keeps parent context small; matches the file-handoff contract |
| Model identity, cost, and latency were **not** in the artifact | **gap** | I recovered them from `session.jsonl` (`openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`, $0.0296 / $0.0106) |
| A `subagent` call with no `task` still spawned a running child | **minor robustness gap** | It had to be steered with the task afterward. This is the Pi subagent layer, not Feynman's research logic |
| The workflow did not create `CHANGELOG.md` automatically | **expected** | `AGENTS.md` says not to create it for one-shot tasks; this run was multi-step, so I created one manually |
| The provenance sidecar is hand-written free text | **structural gap** | `PASS` is an assertion by the agent being evaluated, not a machine-checked result |

The last row is the one I would fix first. A provenance file that cannot independently attest to model, settings, cost, and check outcomes is a lab notebook, not an audit log.

---

## 7. Verdict against the eight dimensions

| Dimension | Assessment | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| D1 Construct validity | **Partial** | The stated construct ("evidence over fluency," auditable artifacts) is clear, but success is operationalised as artifact existence + citation resolution, not claim correctness |
| D2 Task/outcome validity | **Partial, with positive probe evidence** | The verifier's outcome rule is well-posed; the probe shows it can execute; no task-validity argument that the test set represents real drafts |
| D3 Statistical reliability | **Absent** | Single pass per stage; no variance, `pass^k`, or repeated-run reporting |
| D4 Reproducibility/provenance | **Strong artifacts, weak metadata** | Mandatory artifact chain and two-index checks are real; model/seed/temperature/cost are unrecorded |
| D5 Contamination/holdout | **Weak for the harness itself** | Reviewer checks papers for leakage; no holdout or contamination control for the harness's own eval |
| D6 Judge validity | **Absent** | Verifier and reviewer are uncalibrated LLM judges; no agreement benchmark |
| D7 Cost/effort | **Absent from artifacts** | Recoverable from session logs, not reported in provenance |
| D8 Adversarial controls | **Absent as a built-in** | No seeded-defect suite in CI; this study's probes are ad hoc and not shipped |

**Overall:** a harness with an unusually strong *policy* layer and a thin *measurement* layer. It is good at producing artifacts that look auditable; it is not yet set up to prove that its audits work.

---

## 8. Recommendations

Ordered by expected value per unit of engineering effort.

1. **Ship a seeded-defect regression suite.** Use the 15-item instrument in `experiments/verifier-probe/` as a starting point. Run it on every model, prompt, or agent-contract change. Report defect detection and control preservation separately, so a verifier that deletes everything cannot score well.
2. **Make provenance machine-checkable.** Add a structured block: model/provider, temperature, seed, token counts, cost, tool endpoints, artifact SHA-256, and the result of each named check. Today all of this is recoverable from `session.jsonl`; none of it is in the deliverable.
3. **Add repeated-run reliability.** Run the verifier and reviewer 3–5 times on the same draft and report agreement. A single pass cannot distinguish a reliable gate from a lucky one.
4. **Calibrate the judges.** Build a small human-labelled set of claim–source pairs (supported / unsupported / ambiguous) and report the verifier's precision, recall, and agreement. CiteAudit [15] is a public starting point.
5. **Add retraction and correction checks.** OpenAlex already returns `isRetracted`; Crossref exposes update relations. A "verified" citation to a retracted paper is a false pass.
6. **Separate "resolves" from "supports" in the `/lit` metric.** The release note's "44 of 44 citations resolved with matching titles" [12] is a URL/metadata metric. Add a claim-support metric, even if it is sampled and human-audited.
7. **Add a per-run canary.** Plant one known-false claim in a scratch file on every run and confirm the pipeline removes it. This is cheap continuous assurance that the gate is live.
8. **Report retrieval quality per run.** Record which index answered, whether a fallback occurred, and how many queries returned zero records. A zero-result query is a silent evidence gap, not a neutral event.

content.text:
Done. The case study is at **`outputs/feynman-harness-eval-quality.md`** (291 lines), with a provenance sidecar and all raw probe artifacts on disk.

**What I did**

- Built an 8-dimension rubric from the eval-science literature (construct validity, task/outcome validity, variance, reproducibility, contamination, judge validity, cost, adversarial controls).
- Audited the shipped harness mechanisms against it: 4 agents, 11 prompts, 16 skills, 13 extension registrars.
- Dogfooded the `verifier` agent twice with seeded-defect drafts and pre-written oracles.
- Probed the default literature-search tool on 5 fixed queries.

**Headline findings**

| Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Strong *policy* layer, thin *measurement* layer | Written citation rules are specific and testable; no shipped eval suite, no repeated runs, no judge calibration |
| Verifier reconciliation is strong under favorable conditions | Probe 1: 10/10 defects, 5/5 controls. Probe 2: 6/6 defects, 4/4 controls, 0 false removals; $0.0296 / $0.0106, ~45–53 s |
| Retrieval defaults are unstable for multi-concept queries | Semantic Scholar-only: 5/10 returned records relevant; 2 of 4 queries returned zero records. The OpenAlex fallback rescued one rate-limited query at 5/5 |
| Silent failure is invisible | Provenance is self-reported free text; model, cost, seeds, and judge agreement are not recorded. I recovered them from `session.jsonl` |
| Repair > deletion | Probe 2 found the real Deep Research Bench ID (2506.06287) and retained the claim rather than removing it |

**Two self-corrections worth flagging**

1. Probe 1 was confounded — I had pre-loaded the correct numbers into `sources.md`, so it tested reconciliation, not independent verification. Probe 2 used an empty research file to fix that.
2. My own bookkeeping was wrong: I initially reported Probe 2 as 5/5 defects and 5/5 controls. A recount showed 6 defects and 4 controls. Fixed everywhere before delivery.

**Honest limits:** one model (`deepseek-v4.1-flash`), one run per probe, dense synthetic defects, unblinded oracle, and the `reviewer` agent was never tested. The result is evidence that the verifier's contract is executable, not that it is reliable.

**Next step:** run `/deepresearch` end-to-end on a frozen topic and audit its own artifact chain against the same rubric — that would test workflow conformance, which this study deliberately skipped.
